name: Balochi
description: Balochi is a Northwestern Iranian language spoken in southeastern Iran and across a wider region encompassing Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gulf communities. Its regional varieties, oral literature, and developing written standards reveal connections that extend beyond national borders. [s1][s2]

seo.title: Balochi: Language, Regional Varieties and Literature in Iran
seo.description: Explore Balochi in Iran: its Northwestern Iranian roots, regional speech varieties, oral literature, and efforts to develop shared written standards.

content.heading: An Iranian language across borders
content.content:
Balochi, also spelled Baluchi, belongs to the Northwestern Iranian branch of the Indo-European language family. Here, “Iranian” describes linguistic ancestry rather than citizenship. Although southeastern Iran is an important part of its present geography, the language also has substantial connections with southwestern Pakistan, Afghanistan, and communities around the Gulf. Its classification therefore cannot be inferred simply from its position on a modern map. [s1][s2]

For international readers, Balochi is best approached as a language with its own regional traditions rather than as a local form of Persian. Historical comparisons identify relationships with other Iranian languages, while contemporary research emphasizes the diversity of its multilingual surroundings. National borders divide its speakers among different language environments without defining the language's full extent. [s1][s2]

content.heading: Regional varieties and grammatical differences
content.content:
A widely used broad classification distinguishes Western, Southern, and Eastern Balochi, each containing further variation. These are useful groupings rather than a claim that every speaker within a group uses identical forms. Earlier scholarship employed a more detailed division that separately identified varieties such as Rakhshani, Sarawani, Lashari, Kechi, and coastal speech. Readers comparing reference works should recognize that these descriptions operate at different levels of classification. [s1][s2][s3]

Balochi generally places the verb at the end of a clause, but its varieties differ in how they organize other grammatical relationships. Research contrasts past-tense ergative patterns in Coastal Balochi with accusative patterns in Sistani Balochi. In accessible terms, varieties can differ in how they grammatically mark the participants in an action. A description based on one locality should consequently not be treated as a universal grammar of Balochi. [s2]

content.heading: Oral literature and the growth of writing
content.content:
Balochi has an extensive oral literary inheritance, including poetry preserved in different regional varieties. Early published collections represented only portions of that inheritance: Elfenbein cautioned that the prominence of Eastern Hill material in early collecting gave readers a restricted impression of the wider tradition. The history of publication is therefore also a history of which speakers and places collectors documented. [s3]

Written development has involved choices about both script and grammar. Uppsala University's account of Carina Jahani's grammar describes a collaborative standardization programme launched in 2012. An orthography conference in 2014 pursued parallel Arabic-based and Latin-based writing systems; a grammar conference followed in 2016. The resulting 2019 grammar presents proposals developed through consultation with writers and linguists. These milestones document an effort to build shared conventions, rather than proving that all speakers or publishers adopted a single standard. [s1]

content.heading: Understanding the language through its varieties
content.content: The most useful starting point is to ask where a recording, poem, or grammatical description comes from and which writing conventions it follows. Regional speech, inherited oral genres, and a proposed written standard illuminate different aspects of Balochi. Keeping them distinct makes it easier to appreciate both the language's shared foundations and the variety of ways its speakers use it. [s1][s2][s3]

name: Turkmen
description: Turkmen is an Oghuz Turkic language spoken in Iran as well as Turkmenistan and Afghanistan. Regional varieties, contact with Persian, and different writing traditions connect Iranian Turkmen to a wider linguistic world. [s1][s2]

seo.title: Turkmen in Iran: Language, Dialects and Writing Traditions
seo.description: Discover Turkmen's Oghuz Turkic background, regional varieties, Persian connections, and the writing traditions used in Iran and Turkmenistan.

content.heading: Turkmen in Iran's linguistic landscape
content.content:
Turkmen belongs to the Oghuz group of Turkic languages. Its presence in Iran illustrates an essential distinction: a language spoken in Iran need not belong to the Iranian language family. Turkmen's linguistic ancestry connects it with other Turkic languages, while its history also includes sustained interaction with Persian. [s1]

The language extends beyond a single national setting. Indiana University's language portal identifies communities in Iran and Afghanistan alongside those in Turkmenistan, and names Yomut among varieties spoken in Iran. For readers encountering Turkmen through travel, literature, or family histories, the country associated with a speaker or text provides useful context, but does not identify every feature of their speech. [s2]

content.heading: How the language is organized
content.content:
Two features offer a practical introduction to Turkmen grammar. Vowel harmony means that vowels in suffixes adjust to the vowels of the stem. Agglutination means that grammatical information is expressed through suffixes attached in an ordered sequence. These patterns help explain why a Turkmen word can carry information that English distributes across several separate words. [s2]

Long and short vowels are another important part of Turkmen's sound system. Iranica uses this distinction when explaining why neighboring Khorasan Turkic should be treated separately rather than simply grouped under Turkmen. Geographical proximity and related ancestry do not remove meaningful structural differences between languages. [s1]

content.heading: Persian connections and literary history
content.content:
Contact with Persian has contributed both vocabulary and elements used in word formation. Iranica distinguishes direct Persian borrowing from words transmitted through Chaghatay, a historical Turkic literary language. It also separates borrowing from spoken Persian from borrowing through literary usage. These routes matter because similar-looking words can reflect different histories of exchange. [s1]

The same reference account associates the emergence of an eighteenth-century Turkmen literary idiom with Azadi and his son Makhtumquli. Persian elements were present in that literary development from an early stage. Shared vocabulary therefore records cultural and educational connections; it does not change Turkmen's classification as Turkic. [s1]

content.heading: One language, different writing traditions
content.content:
Writing systems introduce a further distinction between communities. Indiana University's account describes Arabic-script usage in Iran and Afghanistan, alongside the Latin alphabet used in Turkmenistan. It traces the Soviet-era sequence from Arabic to Latin and then Cyrillic writing, followed by the reintroduction of Latin writing in the post-Soviet period. That sequence concerns a particular political and educational history and should not be transferred wholesale to Iran. [s2]

For a newcomer, the practical lesson is to identify both the regional variety and the script of a resource. Recognizing spoken words does not automatically confer the ability to read them in another alphabet. Turkmen in Iran is consequently best understood through its combination of local speech, cross-border relationships, and distinct literacy traditions. [s1][s2]

name: Talysh
description: Talysh, also called Taleshi or Talyshi, is a Northwestern Iranian language spoken in northwestern Iran and the Republic of Azerbaijan. Its northern, central, and southern varieties form a dialect continuum shaped partly by contact with neighboring languages. [s1][s2]

seo.title: Talysh in Iran: Regional Varieties and Language Contact
seo.description: Explore Talysh's northern, central, and southern varieties, its multilingual surroundings, and research on grammar and intergenerational transmission.

content.heading: A language extending across a border
content.content:
Talysh is a Northwestern Iranian language encountered in scholarship under spellings including Taleshi and Talyshi. It is spoken in northwestern Iran and across the border in the Republic of Azerbaijan. Linguists conventionally distinguish northern, central, and southern clusters using differences in vocabulary, sounds, and grammar. These labels describe linguistic patterns rather than three self-contained national languages. [s1][s2]

Northern Talysh is particularly important for understanding why the international border is not a dialect boundary. Northern varieties occur in Azerbaijan and also in Iran. Anbarani, spoken in Anbaran and adjacent villages in Ardabil province, is an Iranian example. A description of “Iranian Talysh” therefore needs to include more than the central and southern clusters. [s1]

content.heading: Variation along a continuum
content.content:
Daniel Paul's comparative research examined Anbarani, Asalemi, and Masali as representatives of the northern, central, and southern areas. The study describes a dialect continuum: linguistic features change across the region rather than dividing neatly into wholly separate systems. Its evidence came from fieldwork in Iran, including elicited words and sentences and recorded narratives. [s2]

The surrounding languages help explain some of that variation. Paul's account identifies contact with South Azerbaijani, Tati, Gilaki, and Persian. These neighbors belong to different linguistic backgrounds: South Azerbaijani is Turkic, while the others are Western Iranian. Contact consequently needs to be distinguished from ancestry. A borrowed expression or shared construction can reflect multilingual interaction without making the languages genealogically identical. [s2]

content.heading: What grammar reveals
content.content:
A study of Anbarani explains grammatical relationships through case marking and adpositions—words functioning like prepositions or postpositions. The important point for a general reader is that languages distribute meaning differently: a relationship conveyed through an ending in one language may require a separate word or construction in another. The study's account concerns a named Talysh variety and should not erase differences elsewhere in the continuum. [s1]

Research on comparison offers another example. Hakob Avchyan's study examines Anbarani alongside Northern Talyshi varieties in Azerbaijan. Its abstract reports that degrees of comparison are expressed syntactically through adpositions and function words, rather than dedicated morphological comparison markers. It also identifies influence from Persian and Azerbaijani. Everyday expressions of relative size or degree thus provide evidence of both grammatical structure and a history of language contact. [s3]

content.heading: Transmission and the limits of a snapshot
content.content:
Paul's research also reported language shift toward Persian and instances in which Talysh was no longer being passed to the next generation. That finding belongs to research based on fieldwork in 2006 and 2007; it does not supply a current rate of decline across every community. [s2]

The distinction matters when describing a living language. A regional grammar, a recorded narrative, and a survey of family transmission answer different questions. Together, they show why Talysh deserves attention both as a system of related varieties and as a language whose future depends on patterns of everyday use that require continuing, locally grounded research. [s1][s2][s3]
